Credible means worthy of being believed. When something or someone is credible, you have solid, reasonable grounds to trust or believe them — not just a feeling, but actual backing from evidence, logic, track record, or expertise.

Think of it this way: if your very honest, careful friend tells you something happened, their account is credible. If a stranger with a history of lying tells you the same thing, their account is not credible. The event is the same. The believability is different.

"Credible" is used in two slightly different but closely related ways:

1. Believable and trustworthy
This is about a person, source, or piece of information being reliable enough to take seriously. It means: "I have good reason to trust this."

  • "She is a credible witness." → Her testimony can be trusted; she has no reason to lie, and her account is consistent.
  • "That is a credible news source." → It has a track record of accurate, well-researched reporting.
  • "He gave a credible explanation." → His explanation makes sense and is backed up by facts.

2. Convincing enough to be taken seriously as a real possibility
This sense is used especially with threats, claims, or plans. It means: "This is serious enough that it cannot be dismissed."

  • "The army issued a credible threat." → The threat is not empty; there is reason to believe it could actually be carried out.
  • "She made a credible case for changing the policy." → Her argument was strong enough to be genuinely considered.

Both senses share the same foundation: there is enough substance behind something for a reasonable person to take it seriously.
What Makes Something or Someone Credible?

Credibility doesn't come out of thin air. Something earns the label "credible" through one or more of these:

  • Evidence — It is supported by facts, data, or proof.
  • Consistency — The account doesn't contradict itself or other known facts.
  • Expertise or authority — The person speaking has genuine knowledge or training in the area.
  • Track record — The person or source has been honest and accurate in the past.
  • Motive (or lack of one) — The person has no obvious reason to lie or exaggerate.

When these factors are present, credibility is high. When they're absent, credibility collapses.

These words are close in meaning but are not exactly the same. Understanding the differences will sharpen your grasp of "credible."

Credible vs. Believable
Believable is a softer, more casual word. It simply means "easy to believe." A fictional story can be believable. But credible carries more weight — it implies that there is actual substance or grounding behind the claim, not just that it sounds plausible.

A well-written novel character might be believable, but not credible in a court of law.

Credible vs. Plausible
Plausible means "seeming reasonable or possible on the surface." Something plausible could be true. Something credible is more firmly grounded — it doesn't just seem possible, it has enough support to be genuinely trusted or taken seriously. Plausible is about surface appearance; credible goes deeper.

His alibi was plausible — it could have happened — but the detective didn't find it credible because the details didn't hold up under questioning.

Credible vs. Reliable
Reliable means consistently dependable over time. A reliable person always does what they say. Credible is specifically about being believable and trustworthy in what they say or claim, not necessarily about consistency over time.

A new doctor you've never met can be credible based on their qualifications, even though you have no personal history with them to call them reliable yet.

Credible vs. Trustworthy
Trustworthy is about the character of a person — they can be trusted in general. Credible is more specific to a particular claim, account, or statement being worthy of belief. You might find someone generally trustworthy but still not find their specific claim credible if the evidence doesn't support it.

When something or someone is not credible, a reasonable person would have good reasons to doubt or dismiss them. This can happen because:

  • The account contradicts known facts.
  • The person has an obvious motive to lie.
  • There is no supporting evidence.
  • The story keeps changing.
  • The person lacks any relevant knowledge or expertise.

"The committee found the witness's testimony not credible after it was shown to conflict with recorded footage."

The opposite of credible can be expressed as not credible, incredible (in its formal sense), or implausible, depending on the context.

Here are credible used across a wide range of real-world situations so you can see how the word behaves:

  • Journalism: "Always make sure your information comes from a credible source before publishing it."
  • Law: "The jury found the eyewitness credible because her account remained consistent throughout the trial."
  • Politics/Security: "The government responded only after intelligence confirmed a credible threat to national security."
  • Everyday life: "He offered a credible excuse — he had been in the hospital, and he showed us the paperwork."
  • Science: "The research team presented credible evidence linking the chemical to the disease."
  • Acting/Performance: "She delivered a credible performance as a grieving mother." (Here, it means convincing enough to be believed.)
  • Business: "For investors to fund your startup, you need a credible business plan backed by real numbers."

This is perhaps the most important thing to understand about the word.

Credible does not mean correct or true. It means worthy of belief given the available information. Something can be credible and still turn out to be wrong. A story can be not credible and still happen to be true.

A scientist might put forward a credible hypothesis — one backed by strong reasoning and early evidence — that is later disproved. It was still credible at the time.

Think of credibility as your reasonable judgement about whether to believe something, made with the information you currently have. Truth is the final reality. Credibility is your best assessment of it.

Credible means worthy of trust and belief, backed by enough evidence, logic, consistency, or authority that a reasonable person would take it seriously. It applies to people, statements, threats, evidence, sources, and arguments. It is stronger than "believable" or "plausible" because it implies genuine grounding, not just surface appeal. And critically, it is about the reasonableness of believing something, not a guarantee that it is true.
